I know of plenty of people who could write a novel and find the essay way more comfortable, but I don't think it matters too much on the level that I was describing - most people have a different story. And, the way I describe it, the story is the same regardless of what you're doing; it's the mind of the novelist. But, you can read it and think, well, that sounds like a terrible way to go about it, and I'm glad the essayist chose the opposite way. It's what they call free association, a way of thinking that lets you wander off in any direction you want to.
Now, it wouldn't be so weird to describe your world as a mental universe, but what do you do about the weirdness of it? You have to make it look real. So, the idea of the mind as a universe would be the opposite of the scientific view of the mind as a brain, and, the way I wrote it, the essayist would be, by definition, a skeptic of science. I'm guessing that he's already written a lot about what science doesn't know. And, you can describe his position as skeptic of science, but the idea that the mind is a universe is just as likely to be an alternative to scientific views. I don't have to like science in order to write about it in a novel - it doesn't matter what you think, as long as it's true and there aren't any scientific reasons to think otherwise. Just like you don't have to like it to enjoy reading about it in a novel, or to find the work of a novelist entertaining.
But, I wonder, do people like it when science is described as a kind of religion, like you said, but a science that, for most people, they can't agree with? Or, if you are someone who thinks that science is not about facts, but rather about making sense of the world, is that the right way to describe it? And, are those descriptions really compatible with the idea that science is a religion, or an ideology, or whatever? The problem with the scientific view, I think, is that, for many people, it's a matter of opinion - is it a religion, an ideology, an explanatory theory, or what? I don't mean that there is something wrong with that, but I think the question of whether or not science is a religion is a matter of opinion, and I would like to know if you think that science is a religion, and whether or not you think it's a religion that you can disagree with, or agree with, or whether or not it's a religion that's just the way it is. And, the other thing that you said about the mind as a universe, I think you make a good point about it, too. The thing about the mind as a universe is that you're describing the kind of mind that has a universe, so that makes it a kind of religion, but it doesn't seem to be an ideology. I think it makes a lot of sense, and I think it's very interesting to describe the mind as a universe. But, as long as the mind is described as a universe, I think that you can disagree with science, without having to call it that, and that it's possible to describe it as a religion that you don't find appealing, but that doesn't mean that it's a religion that you have to like. I originally used a simple list of 8 goals, but I soon realized that that was only a very shallow summary of what the book is about. As I thought of more things, it got bigger, and I wanted to avoid repeating those goals over and over. There are a few different versions of this goal - that is to say, I may write about one goal for a chapter, and then write about another goal for another chapter, and then write about another goal for another chapter. There is also a goal about why I choose to write about the book in the first place, and a goal about whether I have any plans for continuing this series.

A:

I am not going to say "I like reading." Instead, I like reading about it. I get a kick out of seeing how my ideas are expanded and developed, and the ways in which they come full circle, leading me to a much deeper and richer understanding of my own world and experiences.
As a writer, I have a similar kind of sense of accomplishment. I like putting my thoughts into a story that people can read, and I like seeing the reactions of my readers as a way of measuring my impact. The idea of this series came from a thought I had early on that I thought might be interesting to a lot of people, but that, frankly, hadn't occurred to me when I was a child. I love this idea that it could reach people, and that the people that read it could share in the experience that I have had as a writer.
I like watching as my characters grow and evolve. I feel like one of the best ways to do that is by writing about their lives, and by sharing the stories of the things that I've read or experienced. I think that part of the appeal of science fiction is that, in places where science is still at a preliminary stage, you can be quite open about your ideas. The more you write about what you believe is possible, the less likely you are to be criticized for being an unrealistic optimist.
Another thing that I like about writing, of course, is that it's a creative process, and that I'm able to make up things that make the stories that I write come to life and feel real. I feel like this is one of the reasons that writing is one of the most rewarding professions, because it's such a creative experience that can take you in directions you never would have dreamed of.</s>
